name: Paris
official_name: Paris (French, /pa.ʁi/). Since 1 January 2019 the legal entity is the 'Ville de Paris', a collectivité à statut particulier created by loi n° 2017-257 of 28 February 2017, in the place of both the commune de Paris and the département de Paris (General Code of Local Authorities, art. L. 2512-1, referring to art. 72 of the Constitution). Official geographic codes: commune 75056, department 75, region 11 (Île-de-France). Inhabitants: Parisiens / Parisiennes.
entity_type: Capital city - the capital and primate city of France; simultaneously a French commune, a department, and a 'collectivité à statut particulier' (Ville de Paris) exercising both commune and department competencies, and the préfecture (regional seat) of Île-de-France. Second object required by the question: the Seine, a navigable French river (fleuve) that crosses the city.
country: France (French Republic), metropolitan territory; located in north-central France, in the Île-de-France region.
administrative_status: A unique double rank in France: (a) the commune of Paris (INSEE 75056), subdivided into 20 municipal arrondissements (grouped since the 2020 elections into 17 arrondissement councils, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th being merged into the single 'Paris Centre' sector); (b) the department of Paris (75), whose departmental functions are exercised by the same body, the Conseil de Paris (163 councillors, who elect the Mayor of Paris), since the merger of 1 January 2019; (c) chef-lieu of the region of Île-de-France and seat of the regional préfecture, as well as seat of the state Prefecture of Police (created 1800, with authority over Paris and the inner-suburban departments). Paris is also the central member of the Métropole du Grand Paris (created 1 January 2016; Paris plus the inner-suburb communes organised into 12 établissements publics territoriaux). River side: the Seine through and around the city belongs to the Seine-Normandie hydrographic district (Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie), with navigation managed by Voies navigables de France and upstream flood-defence works by the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs.
is_capital_of_france: Yes. Paris is the capital of France and its largest city, verified against official sources. Basis: it is the permanent seat of the head of state (Élysée Palace), of the Government (Matignon) and of both parliamentary chambers (National Assembly at the Palais-Bourbon, Senate at the Luxembourg Palace) - which is the definition of 'capitale' used in French public law (the city where the highest state authorities sit permanently); it is expressly designated 'capitale ou siège du gouvernement' for France in French state terminology legislation (arrêté du 4 novembre 1993, replacing the arrêté of 14 October 1985); it is the préfecture of Île-de-France; and it is recognised as the capital of France by international organisations (UN, EU). Key nuance: no French constitution, including that of 4 October 1958, contains a capital clause - the status rests on convention plus ordinary statute.
capital_status_details: Paris's capital status rests on constitutional convention plus ordinary legislation, not on any constitutional clause. (1) Silence of the texts: the 1958 Constitution never mentions Paris or a capital, although art. 2 lists the Republic's symbols (language, national emblem, anthem, motto) - the same silence as in every French constitution since 1791. Constitutional scholars (O. Renaudie, Revue française de droit politique; G. Delledonne, Perspectives on Federalism, vol. 16-3, 2024) describe Paris as a 'constitutional unthought-of', so its status is left to ordinary legislation, unlike Spain (art. 5), Germany (art. 22) or Sweden. (2) Written statutory anchors: art. 9 of the constitutional law of 25 February 1875 had fixed the seat of the executive power and of the two chambers at Versailles; the single-article constitutional law of 21 June 1879 (voted by the National Assembly at Versailles on 19 June 1879) repealed that article, and the ordinary law of 22 July 1879 then fixed the seat of the executive and of both chambers at Paris, allocating the Palais-Bourbon to the Chamber of Deputies and the Palais du Luxembourg to the Senate, effective 3 November 1879 (the Senate actually installed itself on 27 November 1879). Article 3 of that same law kept the Versailles premises for meetings of the two houses sitting in National Assembly/Congress - hence the French Congress (presidential election under art. 7, constitutional revision under art. 89, and the High Court) still meets at the Château de Versailles, the main exception to the rule that all institutions sit in Paris. (3) Terminological/official designation: the arrêté du 4 novembre 1993 relatif à la terminologie des noms d'États et de capitales (Journal officiel) gives Paris as 'capitale ou siège du gouvernement' of France, replacing the arrêté of 14 October 1985 which said the same. (4) Territorial-statute basis: loi n° 2017-257 of 28 February 2017 (in force 1 January 2019) created the Ville de Paris as a collectivité à statut particulier under art. 72 of the Constitution (CGCT art. L. 2512-1), after the loi PLM of 31 December 1982 had made Paris both commune and department; special regimes (Prefecture of Police, merged commune-department assembly) reflect the state's particular presence in the capital. (5) Emergency transfers: temporary removals of the seat of the public authorities during crises - Tours and Bordeaux in 1870-71, Bordeaux in 1914 and 1940, Vichy 1940-44, Algiers 1943-44 - and the royal court's installation at Versailles from 6 May 1682 to 1789 never abolished the capital status; in the doctrine summarised in the 1993 arrêté and in constitutional commentary, a provisional transfer is not a change of capital, and the attachment of the capital character to Paris had already been expressed by the royal ordinance of 25 May 1413, which described the Parlement as the 'cour capitale de notre royaume' required to reside continuously in the good city of Paris.
river_running_through: The Seine (French: la Seine, /sɛn/). Confirmed by official sources: the Seine crosses Paris in a broad arc, entering the commune from the south-east between the 12th arrondissement on the right bank and the 13th on the left bank, just downstream of the Pont amont carried by the Boulevard Périphérique, and leaving to the south-west between the 16th (right bank) and the 15th (left bank) at the Pont aval. Ville de Paris states that the river runs 13 km within the city, is 30 m wide at the quai de Montebello (5th) and 200 m at the Pont de Grenelle (15th), is 3.40-5.70 m deep, and is crossed by 37 bridges. The Marne joins it on the right bank at Charenton-le-Pont/Alfortville/Ivry just outside the south-eastern city limits; the small left-bank Bièvre (covered over in the 19th century) is the only other watercourse historically crossing the city itself.
relationship_between_paris_and_seine: (i) Flow path. The Seine enters Paris at its south-eastern limit between the 12th arrondissement (right bank, Bercy) and the 13th (left bank, Tolbiac/Masséna), immediately downstream of the Pont amont (Boulevard Périphérique), runs north-west past Bercy and Gare de Lyon, then swings west through the centre in two large bends (the arc enclosing the Marais), and leaves to the south-west between the 16th (right) and 15th (left) at the Pont aval; the intramuros length is officially given as 13 km. The Paris reach (bief de Paris) is held at a normal surface level of about 26.7 m above sea level (NGF-IGN69); the official gauging station is the Austerlitz gauge (its zero is set at 25.92 m NGF-IGN69), where a normal stage of 1-2 m corresponds to roughly 330 m3/s. (ii) Arrondissements. Ten arrondissements front the river: right bank 12th, 4th, 1st, 8th, 16th; left bank 13th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 15th; the built area north of the river (Rive droite) is about twice that of the Rive gauche. (iii) Islands. Two natural islands, both in the 4th arrondissement, form the historic core: the Île de la Cité (Roman Lutetia; today Notre-Dame, the Sainte-Chapelle, the Conciergerie/Palais de Justice and the Hôtel-Dieu; enlarged from an original 8-9 ha by the joining of the islets à la Gourdaine, aux Juifs and des Vaches when the Pont Neuf was built, 1578-1607) and the Île Saint-Louis (created when the channel separating the Île Notre-Dame from the Île aux Vaches was filled in the early 17th century; named in 1725). A third, artificial Île aux Cygnes was built in 1827 beneath the Pont de Bir-Hakeim (15th/16th); the former Île Louviers was attached to the right bank and is now part of the Parc de Bercy. (iv) Bridges. Thirty-seven bridges cross the Seine within Paris (Ville de Paris, 2025 update), among them the Pont Neuf (1578-1607, the oldest surviving), the Pont Marie and Pont de la Tournelle serving the Île Saint-Louis, the Pont au Change, Pont Notre-Dame, Pont Saint-Michel, Pont au Double, Petit-Pont, Pont d'Arcole and Pont de l'Archevêché around the Île de la Cité, then the Pont des Arts, Pont du Carrousel, Pont Royal, Pont de la Concorde, Pont Alexandre III (1900 Universal Exhibition), Pont d'Iéna (Eiffel Tower), Pont de Bir-Hakeim and Pont de Grenelle (carrying metro line 6 and RER C levels); the last road bridge built was the Pont Charles-de-Gaulle (1996) and the newest crossing is the Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir (2006). Sources differ slightly on the number of pedestrian-only footbridges (four per Ville de Paris, five per the bridge inventory). (v) Heritage articulation. The UNESCO property is precisely the river and its urban interface: the banks, quays and bridges of the historic course between the Pont de Sully and the Pont d'Iéna (365 ha, including 23 of the 37 bridges and both islands) - the city-river relationship is itself the protected value. (vi) Functional links. The bief de Paris is operated by HAROPA PORT-Paris (about 30 urban ports inside the city, river berths from Alfortville to Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, some 200 moored houseboats) on a Grand Gabarit waterway joining Le Havre and Rouen to Gennevilliers and Bercy; the river also carries the city's cruise and leisure traffic, was the historic source of water, power and waste dispersal, and since 5 July 2025 again permits public swimming at three sites (Bercy 12th, Bras Marie/Paris Centre, Bras de Grenelle 15th), a use banned since the 1920s.
location_coordinates: Approximately 48.857 N, 2.352 E (WGS84; the commonly cited reference point is 48 51' 24'' N, 2 21' 07'' E), in the centre of the national territory, north-central France, about 170 km (as the crow flies; over 200 km by river) upstream of the Seine estuary at Le Havre and about 145 km south-east of the English Channel coast. The 'Point zéro des routes de France' (road-distance zero marker) stands on the parvis of Notre-Dame on the Île de la Cité. Elevation: 21 m at the lowest point to 131 m on the butte Montmartre; normal level of the Seine about 26.7 m.
physical_setting: Paris lies at the heart of the Paris Basin - a vast shallow sedimentary (limestone, marl, chalk) basin of fertile plains and low relief - on a loop of the Seine between that river's confluences with the Marne (upstream, right bank) and the Oise (downstream, right bank). The city occupies a wide alluvial valley containing the present river course, the former (pre-Neolithic) northern arm of the Seine (the marshy zone that gave the Marais district its name and that flooded in 1910) and the buried valley of the Bièvre, captured by the Seine in the Neolithic. The valley is ringed by low buttes-témoins: Montmartre 131 m, Belleville 128.5 m, Ménilmontant 108 m, Buttes-Chaumont 103 m, Passy 71 m, Chaillot 67 m on the right bank; Montparnasse 66 m, Butte-aux-Cailles 63 m, Montagne Sainte-Geneviève 61 m on the left. The col de la Chapelle, a low gap between Montmartre and Belleville, has always carried the north-east communications (canals de l'Ourcq and Saint-Martin, Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est). Climate (Météo-France reference station Paris-Montsouris, 75 m, operating since June 1872; 1991-2020 normals): degraded (altéré) oceanic, Köppen Cfb, mean annual temperature 12.8 C (January 5.4 C, July 20.9 C), 634.3 mm of precipitation spread over about 109 rain days with no dry month (wettest May about 69 mm, driest February about 42 mm), light winds (3.2 m/s) and a pronounced urban heat island (night-time minima about +2 C above surrounding forest). This gently sloping, pluvial, downstream-urbanised basin is the physical origin of the flood risk the river poses to the capital.
area_km2: 105.40 km2 of land area for the commune / Ville de Paris (INSEE official geographic figure; 113th largest commune of metropolitan France), a figure that includes the two large intra-city parks, the Bois de Vincennes (12th) and the Bois de Boulogne (16th). For comparison, the former department of the Seine, which Paris headed, covered 480 km2, and the Île-de-France region covers 12,011 km2. River reference: the Seine watershed drains 75,000-78,650 km2 - the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie states 75,000 km2 for the basin it manages, while French hydrographic summaries and the river-basin flood plans give 76,500-78,650 km2, about one seventh of metropolitan France.
river_length_km: The Seine is 776.6 km long, the second-longest river of France after the Loire. [uncertain] Official bodies publish slightly different totals: SANDRE/Bd Topage 775 km, Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie 773 km, Ville de Paris 777 km, Eaufrance summary 776 km; the widely used 776.6 km derives from the SANDRE river reference. Length within Paris: 13 km (official Ville de Paris figure for the intramuros section); some hydrographic GIS measurements give 14.5 km for the stretch lying within the city limits, and the river is inside the Île-de-France region for roughly 100 km.
river_source: The Seine rises on the Plateau de Langres at Source-Seine (commune of Source-Seine, formerly Saint-Germain-Source-Seine, department of Côte-d'Or, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté), at about 47 29' 10'' N, 4 43' 01'' E, where the spring is marked by an artificial grotto holding a statue of the nymph Sequana, a Gallo-Roman cult site. [uncertain] The altitude of the source is given inconsistently by otherwise authoritative sources: 446 m (river databases and French encyclopedic infoboxes), 450 m (Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie), 452 m (regional canoe federation hydrosheet) and 470-472 m (older geographic references and the 2007 Seine flood-plan notice, which says 471 m); the accepted range is therefore roughly 446-471 m. The source is small and the upper course is seasonally variable, which is why the river is hydrographically debatable (its greatest upstream branch by discharge is the Yonne).
river_mouth: The Seine discharges into the English Channel (la Manche) through a tidal estuary about 15 km long, the mouth being conventionally fixed between Le Havre (Seine-Maritime) on the left (south) bank and Honfleur (Calvados) on the right (north) bank, with reference coordinates 49 26' 02'' N, 0 12' 24'' E at 0 m altitude; the estuary widens from about 500 m at Quillebeuf to several kilometres at the Honfleur line, and HAROPA PORT administers Le Havre and Rouen on either side of it. Mean discharge is of the order of 480-500 m3/s near the mouth, against about 330 m3/s at Paris-Austerlitz; the river has no run-of-river dams on its main stem but is regulated by the upstream reservoir lakes.
departments_crossed: Upstream to downstream (13 departments, the standard French hydrographic list): Cote-d'Or (21, about 86 km), Aube (10, about 164 km - the longest stretch), Marne (51, bordered), Seine-et-Marne (77, about 99 km), Essonne (91, about 27 km), Val-de-Marne (94, about 13 km along its southern edge), Paris (75, about 13-14.5 km), Hauts-de-Seine (92, about 20 km), Seine-Saint-Denis (93, about 8 km), Val-d'Oise (95, as a boundary), Yvelines (78, about 97 km), Eure (27, about 101 km) and Seine-Maritime (76, about 102 km, largely as a boundary with Eure), before the estuary touches Calvados (14) at Honfleur. [uncertain] The count itself is disputed because it depends on whether departments merely bordered are counted: Ville de Paris says the Seine crosses 12 departments, hydrographic inventories say 13, the 2007 Seine flood-plan notice says 15 departments are crossed or bordered, and river-basin articles list 14 plus the Yonne within the basin.
major_tributaries: Main direct tributaries, upstream to downstream, with bank stated facing downstream (per the SANDRE-derived lists and the Initiatives River basin synopsis): Ource (right, 100 km), Barse (right, 50 km), Aube (right, 249 km, at Marcilly-sur-Seine, after which the river turns north-west), Yonne (292 km, at Montereau-Fault-Yonne - [uncertain] bank: the hydrographic lists place it on the left, and by the naming rule based on discharge (Yonne 93 m3/s and 10,836 km2 against Seine 80 m3/s and 10,300 km2) the water flowing past Paris is properly the Yonne, making the Seine technically a branch of the Yonne via the Aube, although many general references still describe the Yonne as a right-bank tributary), Loing (left, 143 km, at Saint-Mammès), Essonne (left, 101 km, at Corbeil-Essonnes), Orge (left), Yerres (right, 98 km, Villeneuve-Saint-Georges), Marne (right, 514 km, at Charenton-le-Pont/Alfortville/Ivry, i.e. at the south-eastern edge of Paris - the largest contributor to flood waves reaching the capital), Bièvre (left, buried within Paris), Oise (right, 341 km, at Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, rising in Belgium), Aubette de Meulan (right), Mauldre (left), Vaucouleurs (left), Epte (right, 113 km, at Giverny; the former frontier of Normandy), Andelle (bank given as left by some sources and right by others), Eure (left, 229 km, at Saint-Pierre-lès-Elbeuf) and Risle (left, 145 km, at Berville-sur-Mer in the estuary), plus the small maritime-side Robec and Aubette at Rouen. In all, about 45-47 tributaries are commonly listed, and the Bd Topage hydrographic reference counts 121 direct tributaries, the Marne being the longest.
population_value: 2,103,778 inhabitants - the official 'population municipale' of the commune / Ville de Paris and the most recent authentic figure published by INSEE. Population totale (municipal plus separately counted): 2,119,412 (with 15,634 counted separately). Paris is the most populous commune of France. Context: about 7.1 million inhabitants in the Grand Paris area and about 12.4 million in the Île-de-France region (roughly 19 % of metropolitan France's population) - which is also the population of the Paris basin served by the river.
population_date: Millésime 2023 (population as of 1 January 2023, in commune boundaries in force 1 January 2025) - INSEE's 'populations de référence 2023', the newest officially authentic series in force on the date of this research: in force 1 January 2026, authenticated by decree n° 2025-1362 of 26 December 2025, published 29 December 2025. Issuing statistical office: Insee (Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques), annual census method, 2023 main survey; the same 2,103,778 figure and the 2023 density are repeated in the INSEE 'Dossier complet' for Paris refreshed 27 August 2026. The next vintage (millésime 2024) is normally decreed in late December and was not yet available on 27 November 2026.
population_density: 19,959.9 inhabitants per km2 (2023; INSEE official computation on the 105.40 km2 area, commonly rounded to 19,960 hab/km2) - by far the densest large French commune, against about 168 hab/km2 for France as a whole and about 1,030 hab/km2 for Île-de-France. INSEE historical series for Paris on identical boundaries: 24,580 hab/km2 (1968) falling to 19,959.9 (2023), tracking the population decline from 2,590,771 (1968) to 2,103,778 (2023), an average change of -0.6 % per year over 2017-2023 (natural balance +0.5 %, apparent migration balance -1.2 %).
capital_designation_history: (1) Origins on the river. The Celtic Parisii occupied the Seine loop (the Bercy excavations show Mediterranean contacts by the 7th century BC); Caesar refers to Lutetia as an oppidum of the Parisii situated on an island of the Seine, and in 52 BC his legate Labienus captured and burned it; the Gallo-Roman town grew on the Île de la Cité and on the Left Bank (Montagne Sainte-Geneviève), and the guild of the nautes (river shipowners; see the 1st-century Pilier des Nautes) dominated its commerce. (2) First capital. After his victories over the Alamans and Visigoths Clovis I chose Paris as his capital about 508, resided there and died there in 511; under the Merovingians the city kept that rank for about a century. The Carolingians neglected it (Aachen being the imperial seat) and Paris was burned by the Vikings in 857 and besieged in 885-886, repelled by Bishop Gozlin and Count Odo, ancestor of the Capetians as counts of Paris. (3) Capetian fixation. The election of Hugh Capet (987), count of Paris, attached the dynasty to the town, but the early Capetians still shared their residences between Senlis, Étampes, Orléans and Paris; only under Louis VI (1108-1137) and Louis VII (1137-1180) did Paris definitively prevail over Orléans and Saint-Denis become the royal necropolis, and Philip Augustus (1180-1223) supplied the real apparatus of a capital - the Louvre fortress, enclosure walls, paving of the streets, the royal archives and treasury at the Palais de la Cité, the University, the Halles. Hence the standard description of an uncontested capital from the 12th century, reinforced by the royal ordinance of 25 May 1413 calling the Parlement the 'cour capitale de notre royaume' and requiring it to reside continuously in Paris. By 1297 the city held some 200,000 people, the largest in western Europe. (4) Rival seat. Louis XIV installed his court and the government at Versailles on 6 May 1682, which remained the effective centre of the kingdom until 1789 - yet, as the Château de Versailles itself states, Paris never lost its title of capital. The forced return of Louis XVI and the Constituent Assembly to Paris in October 1789 reasserted the city's political capital status, maintained under the Consulate and Empire (Tuileries), the Restoration, the monarchy of July, the Second Republic and Second Empire, when Haussmann rebuilt the river frontage. (5) The only legal rupture, 1870-1879. After Sedan (2 September 1870) the Republic was proclaimed at the Hôtel de Ville; the Government of National Defence withdrew to Tours and then Bordeaux while Paris was besieged; the elected Assembly sat at Bordeaux and then Versailles, and during the Commune (March-May 1871) the government stayed at Versailles. Article 9 of the constitutional law of 25 February 1875 formally fixed the seat of the executive and of the two chambers at Versailles. The constitutional law of 21 June 1879 repealed art. 9, and the ordinary law of 22 July 1879 fixed the seat at Paris from 3 November 1879 (Chamber at the Palais-Bourbon, Senate at the Luxembourg from 27 November), which Gambetta hailed as restoring to 'our incomparable capital the legal title of which it had been too long deprived'; Congresses, however, remained at Versailles, where the French Congress still convenes. (6) Twentieth century. Paris remained the capital through both world wars, with emergency government transfers to Bordeaux in 1914 and 1940 and the Vichy regime (1940-44, never recognised as legitimate) while Free France sat at Brazzaville and then Algiers; full republican authority returned with the Liberation of Paris on 25 August 1944, and from 1958 the Fifth Republic has kept all constitutional organs in Paris (except the Congress). (7) Present statutory framework. The capital role is combined with an administrative status repeatedly reformed by ordinary law: the loi PLM of 31 December 1982, the reorganisation of the Paris region under loi n° 64-707 of 10 July 1964 (effective 1 January 1968, which abolished the departments of the Seine and Seine-et-Oise), the creation of the Métropole du Grand Paris (2016) and loi n° 2017-257 creating the single Ville de Paris collectivity (1 January 2019).
historical_role_of_river: The Seine is the reason for, and the spine of, the capital. (a) Site and defence. A chain of islands made this point the natural crossing of one of western Europe's great waterway axes, at the junction of the Seine, Marne, Oise (and the now-buried Bièvre) and at the northern road gap of the col de la Chapelle; Caesar took the island oppidum in 52 BC, the population retreated onto the fortified island in the 3rd-4th centuries (wall of 308, thermal baths), Charles the Bald restored the City wall and fortified the single bridge against the Vikings (884-886), and the marshy former northern arm of the river fixed the line of medieval ramparts and gave the Marais its name. (b) Trade and municipal power. The river drove medieval prosperity: the guild of the nautes, then the 'marchands de l'eau', claimed the monopoly of Paris river trade from the late 11th century (confirmed by Philip Augustus) as far as Rouen, judged disputes at the Parloir aux Bourgeois on the place de Grève, and from the mid-13th century provided the prévôt des marchands, who with the king's prévôt de Paris (at the Châtelet) ran the city in a distinctive two-headed government (from 1266). The port de la Grève was a principal economic centre, carrying wine, grain, firewood by flottage, stone and timber, although navigation was then possible only four to six months a year and was choked by bridges and mills. The galley of this guild remains the city's arms, with the motto 'Fluctuat nec mergitur'. (c) Urban growth and infrastructure. Quays were built progressively from the royal orders of 1607 and 1623 and completed in the early 19th century; Haussmann regularised the banks and rebuilt bridges (and covered the Bièvre); the Seine fed the canals de l'Ourcq, Saint-Martin and Saint-Denis, supplied water, power and a sink for waste, hosted some 80 washing-boats by the 18th century and passenger 'bateaux-coches' to Melun or Sens, and fronted the Universal Exhibitions of 1855, 1867, 1878, 1889 (Eiffel Tower), 1900 (Pont Alexandre III, Grand and Petit Palais) and 1937 (Trocadéro). (d) Floods as a planning driver. After 1910 the state raised quays and bridges in Paris to the 1910 level, dredged the channel downstream, built anti-flood parapets (murettes) in the former department of the Seine from 1936, and in 1926 the programme of upstream reservoir lakes was launched. (e) Naming of departments. The river gave its name to the department of the Seine (created 4 March 1790 as the département de Paris, renamed Seine on 22 August 1795 - the BnF notices 11 October 1795 - and suppressed on 1 January 1968 under loi n° 64-707 of 10 July 1964, split into Paris 75, Hauts-de-Seine 92, Seine-Saint-Denis 93 and Val-de-Marne 94), to Seine-et-Marne (77), to Seine-et-Oise (78, replaced in 1968 by Yvelines, Essonne and Val-d'Oise) and to Seine-Inférieure, which by decree of 18 January 1955 became Seine-Maritime (76).
government_institutions_located: All the principal national seats are in Paris, with one institutional exception. Head of state and government: the President of the Republic at the Palais de l'Élysée (8th arrondissement); the Prime Minister at the Hôtel de Matignon (7th). Parliament: the National Assembly at the Palais-Bourbon (7th, assigned by the law of 22 July 1879), its president residing at the Hôtel de Lassay; the Senate at the Palais du Luxembourg (6th), its president in the Petit Luxembourg. The exception: the two houses sitting together as the National Assembly/Congress - for the election of the President (art. 7) and for constitutional revision (art. 89) - and the High Court meet at the Château de Versailles (art. 3 of the law of 22 July 1879). Independent and supreme jurisdictions: the Constitutional Council at 2 rue de Montpensier, in the Palais-Royal (1st); the Council of State (Conseil d'État) and the Court of Auditors (Cour des comptes), also in the Palais-Royal (1st); the Court of Cassation at the Palais de la Cité on the Île de la Cité (1st), alongside the Paris Court of Appeal and the Court of Justice of the Republic. Central ministries concentrated in Paris include Foreign Affairs (Quai d'Orsay, 7th), Economy and Finance (Bercy, 12th), Armed Forces (Balard, 15th) and the Interior (Place Beauvau, 8th), together with the Prefecture of Police, the Bank of France (1st), the Institut de France (6th) and the headquarters of national media and learned academies. Regional and local seats: the Préfecture de la région Île-de-France, the Île-de-France Regional Council and the Hôtel de Ville (4th), which is the meeting place of the Conseil de Paris.
administrative_divisions: City side: Paris is divided into 20 municipal arrondissements, numbered in a spiral from the Louvre, each with an arrondissement council and a mayor (not full mayors: they hold powers delegated by the Mayor of Paris and are officers of civil status); the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th have shared a single council, 'Paris Centre', since the 2020 elections, giving 17 arrondissement assemblies while the 20 arrondissements remain the official subdivisions (and the basis of postal codes 75001-75020). The assembly of the collectivity, the Conseil de Paris, has 163 members (with 340 arrondissement councillors; 503 local elected officials in total), and below it are the quartier councils and the administrative quartiers used for statistics. For state purposes Paris is still department 75 with a single arrondissement (the commune itself). Above it stand the Métropole du Grand Paris (2016; its 12 établissements publics territoriaux) and the Île-de-France region (8 departments). River side (Seine governance): the Seine falls within France's twelve hydrographic districts, specifically the Bassin Seine-Normandie (about 75,000 km2), whose water agency is the Agence de l'eau Seine-Normandie (created 1964) and whose planning instrument is the SDAGE Seine-Normandie; flood-peak smoothing and low-flow support on the reservoir lakes upstream of Île-de-France are the responsibility of the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs (successor to the interdepartmental reservoir body created in 1926; four lakes today, a fifth under construction); navigation on the river and canal network is run by Voies navigables de France; the ports of the Paris reach by HAROPA PORT; flood forecasting by the 'Seine Moyenne Yonne Loing' forecast service of the DRIEAT Île-de-France within the national Vigicrues system; bathing-water sanitary control by the ARS Île-de-France; land-use flood regulation by the PPRI of Paris (revised 2007, annexed to the PLU); and the cross-cutting flood-prevention programme PAPI of the Seine and Marne in Île-de-France (2023-2029, about EUR 133 million) coordinated by the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs.
economic_significance: Paris and Île-de-France are by far France's leading economy and among the world's largest regional economies. Latest official regional accounts (Insee, published May 2026, provisional 2024 data): regional GDP of EUR 865.7 billion in current values, i.e. 30.2 % of the GDP of metropolitan France (EUR 2,863.0 billion) - about a third of national wealth produced by 18.8 % of the metropolitan population and 23.5 % of employment - making Île-de-France the richest EU region in purchasing-standard terms (EUR 797 billion PPS), ahead of Nordrhein-Westfalen and above Belgium or Ireland; GDP per inhabitant EUR 69,514 in 2024 (against EUR 43,170 for metropolitan France, roughly +87 % over the provinces) and GDP per job EUR 123,220 (+41 %); the Insee analysis n° 229 of 10 November 2026 is headlined 'l'Île-de-France concentre près d'un tiers de la richesse métropolitaine'. The economy is highly tertiarised (88.4 % of regional value added from services, against 79.8 % nationally), concentrates the largest body of group headquarters in Europe, and is France's leading foreign-trade region (23.6 % of French goods exports and 28.3 % of imports in 2024, CCI Paris Île-de-France), with finance, law, consulting, luxury, media, research and higher education concentrated in the city. Port and inland-waterway role: the Seine is the logistics spine of this economy. HAROPA PORT, the single Le Havre-Rouen-Paris authority created on 1 June 2021, is France's first port (102 Mt handled in 2024); its Paris division runs the river reach, with Gennevilliers (401 ha, more than 250 firms, 8,000 direct jobs, France's first river container terminal - 130,895 EVP in 2023 and about 500,000 EVP movements via Paris Terminal in 2024, and a leading cement port), Bonneuil-sur-Marne (second multimodal platform in the region), Limay-Porcheville, plus about 30 urban ports inside Paris, some 40 river berths between Alfortville and Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, shared-use quays and about 200 houseboats. River freight on the Seine axis exceeds 22 Mt a year (the Seine basin taking 40-50 % of all French river freight, about 18 Mt in 2023, mostly construction materials 59 % and cereals 18.6 %) and about 80 % of French river-tourism activity; more than 270,000 EVP moved on the Seine in 2024, with the Le Havre-Gennevilliers shuttle up 20 % and a 13 % river modal share for containers at HAROPA PORT. Policy treats the waterway as under-used (no saturation, 99.5 % availability, open 24/7, half of the 700+ km of the axis at Grand Gabarit class) and tourism is a co-equal pillar, with EUR 23.6 billion of tourist spending in 2025.
cultural_heritage_sites: The listing that ties the two objects together is UNESCO's 'Paris, Banks of the Seine' (World Heritage List No. 600, later 600bis after an approved minor boundary modification), inscribed in 1991 by the 15th session of the World Heritage Committee under criteria (i), (ii) and (iv), with a retrospective Statement of Outstanding Universal Value adopted in 2017 (decision 41 COM 8E). The property is the river and its urban interface: the bridges, quays and banks of the historic course between the Pont de Sully and the Pont d'Iéna, together with the Île de la Cité and the Île Saint-Louis - 365 hectares including 23 of the 37 Paris bridges (Ville de Paris). The Committee's synthesis calls it 'an exceptional and unique example of urban riverside architecture' in which the layers of the history of the capital of one of Europe's first great nation states are harmoniously superposed, and names the masterpieces it protects: Notre-Dame and the Sainte-Chapelle (source of the spread of Gothic architecture), the Louvre, the Institut de France, the Invalides, the Place de la Concorde, the École Militaire, the Monnaie, the Grand Palais, the Pont Neuf, the Eiffel Tower and the Palais de Chaillot, the coherent ensembles of the Marais, the Île Saint-Louis, the quai Malaquais and quai Voltaire, and Haussmann's squares and avenues, which influenced town planning worldwide (including Latin America); it also notes the age-old upstream/downstream division of functions (port and river transport upstream, royal and aristocratic Paris downstream) and flags vulnerability to urban development, traffic pollution and tourism. The property was inscribed without a buffer zone and was examined under the Committee's state-of-conservation procedure in the run-up to the 2024 Olympic Games, which accelerated investment in river water quality. On-the-ground protection combines the historic-monuments classification of quays, bridges and riverfront buildings, the Paris PLU, the PPRI, and the wider protected landscapes of the Seine valley (regional natural parks of the Boucle de la Seine and the Grands Lacs). Within the city this is the single UNESCO inscription; the nearest other French listing is the Palace of Versailles (1979), outside Paris.
tourism_and_landmarks: Paris-Île-de-France is the world's leading urban destination and its riverfront carries most of the icons. Latest official annual balance (Visit Paris Region / Choose Paris Region and CCI Paris Île-de-France, published March and October 2026): 49.1 million tourists in Île-de-France in 2025 (+1 % on the Olympic year 2024), including a record 23.2 million international visitors (+3 %) and 25.9 million French visitors, generating a record EUR 23.6 billion of tourist spending. On the narrower Grand Paris perimeter, the city's tourism office (Paris je t'aime) counts 37.3 million tourists in 2025, and INSEE records about 47.2 million nights in collective tourist accommodation in the commune of Paris in 2025 (+9.5 %) - the three perimeters must not be added. Sites on or beside the water, 2025: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Paris about 11 million visitors in the year following its reopening on 7 December 2024 (10.9 million in the CCI 2025 table; some 8-9 million a year before the 2019 fire; its towers, reopened in September 2025, drew 110,017 visitors by the end of 2025); Musée du Louvre about 9.0 million (the world's most visited museum); Tour Eiffel 6,744,211 visitors admitted to its levels (a record, +450,000 on 2024) plus nearly 10 million people on the free esplanade (SETE, 7 January 2026); Grand Palais 3.50 million; Musée d'Orsay 3.79 million per CCI (the city's tourism office publishes 4.9 million for 2025 on a different counting basis - discrepancy noted); Arc de Triomphe 1.85 million; Musée de l'Armée/Invalides 1.40 million; Musée du quai Branly-Jacques Chirac 1.39 million; Sainte-Chapelle 1.33 million on the Île de la Cité; Conciergerie 0.77 million; Fondation Louis Vuitton 1.57 million. River-based activity is itself a major product: more than 9 million passengers a year travel the Seine in the Paris region on sightseeing and overnight cruises, the river hosted the Olympic triathlon and marathon-swimming events in 2024, and public swimming was reopened on 5 July 2025 at Bercy (12th), the Bras Marie (Paris Centre) and the Bras de Grenelle (15th), after a ban in force since the 1920s. Other river-linked landmarks: Pont Alexandre III, Pont Neuf, the Tuileries and the Berges de Seine promenades (left-bank riverside road closed to through traffic in 2022, right-bank expressway removed), Paris Plages, the Île Saint-Louis and the artificial Île aux Cygnes with its miniature Statue of Liberty.
flood_risk_management: Paris is a flood-exposed capital and a Seine flood is one of the largest single catastrophe risks in Europe. (a) Reference event: the Great Flood of 1910 - after an exceptionally wet autumn 1909 and renewed January 1910 rains on saturated, partly frozen soils, the Marne, upper Seine, Aube, Yonne and Loing flood waves coincided, and the river peaked at 8.62 m on the Austerlitz gauge on 28 January 1910, with a discharge of 2,400 m3/s against about 330 m3/s normally - the highest level since 1658. Some 720 hectares of Paris were inundated, about 20,000 buildings were damaged, direct damage ran to about 400 million gold francs, the Métro was out of use until early April, with roughly 10 days of high water and 35 days of recession; the OECD (2014) assessed a repeat today at tens of billions of euros (a figure widely reported as about EUR 30 billion). Other notable events: 1924, 1955 (7.28 m), 1958, 1966, 1982, 1995, 1999-2001, the June 2016 'warning shot' (6.10 m at Austerlitz, metro and RER C stations closed as a precaution, damage concentrated in the unprotected outer suburbs on the Loing, Ouanne, Yerres, Orge and Essonne) and the January 2018 flood, when the reservoir lakes lowered the Paris water level by about 65 cm. (b) Structural prevention upstream: the reservoir lakes managed by the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs - Seine (Lac d'Orient, in service 1966, 207.8 Mm3), Marne (Lac du Der-Chantecoq, 1974, 350 Mm3), Aube (Lac du Temple and Lac Amance, 1990, 170.3 Mm3) and Yonne (Pannecière, the oldest), plus EDF's Crescent and Bois-Chaumeçon gates - give cumulative storage of about 805-850 Mm3 (sources give 805, 807 or 850 million m3), over 80 % of the 1926 target. They smooth flood peaks but control only 17 % of the area upstream of Paris and their filling/emptying cycle runs from 1 July to 1 November, so for a 1910-type event the expected reduction at Paris is only about 65-70 cm from the lakes and about 1.0-1.2 m once all local works and channel improvements are counted; a fifth reservoir lake on the Voire is under construction, and the Bassée alluvial flood-retention project on the Seine floodplain (expected to lower Paris levels by 20-40 cm) is under study. (c) Structural prevention in and near the city: after 1910 the state raised quays and bridges inside Paris to the 1910 level (8.60 m) and dredged the channel downstream to improve conveyance; from 1936 anti-flood parapets (murettes) were built along the banks of the former department of the Seine, set above the 1924 level (7.30 m) with 20-30 cm of freeboard; the embankments built after 1924 between Choisy-le-Roi and Gennevilliers proved effective in 2016. In Paris, movable defences - stop-logs (batardeaux, the first installed from 3.70 m), flood barriers and parapet extensions, including the system serving the Invalides/Ecole Militaire frontage - are deployed when the river approaches 5 m at Austerlitz with a major-flood risk. (d) Non-structural measures: permanent gauging on the Austerlitz scale (zero = 25.92 m NGF-IGN69) by the DRIEAT Île-de-France flood-forecast service 'Seine Moyenne Yonne Loing' within the national Vigicrues system, with the level sent daily to the Prefecture of Police and passed to the city's operational watch as soon as 2.50 m is reached; the flood-risk prevention plan (PPRI) of Paris, revised in 2007 and annexed to the PLU, which zones flood-prone land and requires public-service facilities located there to hold their own flood protection plans; the PAPI of the Seine and Marne in Île-de-France (coordinated by the EPTB Seine Grands Lacs since 2013; the 2023-2029 programme totals about EUR 133 million) funding risk culture, school and public awareness and works; the SEQUANA European crisis exercises (2016); and the water-quality and bathing plan launched in 2016, which invested over EUR 1 billion in sewer separation, boat and floating-building connection and storage capacity - including the Austerlitz retention basin (about 50,000 m3, 13th arrondissement) that prevented sewage overflows during the 2024 Games. (e) Residual vulnerability: Paris intramuros is defended to the 1910 level, but parts of the inner and outer suburbs only to 1982, 1955 or 1924 design levels; a 1910-type flood today would still inundate metro lines and tunnels (including RER C), riverside museums (the Louvre, Orsay and the Jeu de Paume maintain raised galleries and flood shelters), hospitals and critical infrastructure, a risk aggravated since 1910 by massive occupation of floodplains, soil sealing, densification and climate change; the 2016 mission to the Prime Minister concluded that the reservoirs are not an all-risk insurance for Île-de-France.

data_as_of: Research performed on 27 November 2026. Vintage of the newest figures used: Paris population, population totale and density = INSEE reference populations, millésime 2023, authentic decree n° 2025-1362 of 26 December 2025, published 29 December 2025, in force 1 January 2026 (also reproduced in the INSEE 'Dossier complet' refreshed 27 August 2026); regional GDP = Insee regional accounts, provisional 2024 figures published May 2026 and in Insee Analyses Île-de-France n° 229 of 10 November 2026; tourist arrivals and spending = the 2025 annual balance, published March 2026 (Visit Paris Region) and October 2026 (CCI Paris Île-de-France Chiffres-clés 2026-2027); Eiffel Tower attendance = 2025 figures published 7 January 2026; river-freight and port data = 2024 (HAROPA PORT 2024 activity report, VNF 2025 press kit) with basin tonnage for 2022-2023 (CESER Normandie, March 2026); Seine hydrometry, flood history and flood-defence data = Ville de Paris pages updated 2025-2026, EPTB Seine Grands Lacs PAPI 2023-2029, and the November 2016 report to the Prime Minister; climate = Météo-France 1991-2020 normals (sheet issued June 2025); Seine bathing = the 2025 season; administrative status = legislation in force as of 2026 (loi 2017-257, effective 1 January 2019); UNESCO = 1991 inscription, 2017 retrospective statement, ICOMOS report of 13 March 2024.
